lead: The Gibbs phase rule counts how many intensive properties you may choose freely before a system in equilibrium is fixed. For a system without chemical reactions it reads F = C − P + 2, where C is the number of components and P the number of phases present. One line explains why boiling water at a given pressure has only one possible temperature, why the triple point of a pure substance is a single point, and why no pure substance shows four phases together.
prereq: You need: phases, saturation and the triple line from 5.1, and the triple point from 5.2.

sections.h3: Components, phases and degrees of freedom

blocks.text: A component is one of the smallest set of chemical species needed to make up every phase of the system. Water, as ice, liquid or vapour, is one component. Moist air is usually counted as two: dry air (its make-up does not change) and water. The number of components is C.

A phase is a region uniform in composition and physical structure, as in 5.1. Ice, liquid water and water vapour are three phases; a mixture of gases is always one phase, because gases mix completely. The number of phases present together is P.

The degrees of freedom F are the number of intensive properties (temperature, pressure and the composition of each phase) that can be changed independently without making a phase appear or disappear. Some syllabi call F the variance of the system.

blocks.where: F is the number of degrees of freedom; C is the number of components; P is the number of phases in equilibrium; the 2 stands for the two intensive properties every phase shares, temperature and pressure. The rule holds for a system in equilibrium with no chemical reactions.

blocks.text: The rule counts intensive properties only. It says nothing about how much of each phase is present. That is why the dryness fraction of wet steam can still change while F = 1: x measures amounts, not an intensive property of either phase.

Count the unknowns and the equations. Every phase has the same T and p in equilibrium: that is 2 unknowns. Each phase also has C mole fractions, but they add to 1, so only C − 1 of them are free; for P phases that makes P(C − 1) more unknowns.

Equilibrium between phases needs one more condition for each component: it must have the same chemical potential, the Gibbs function per mole, in every phase. Otherwise that component would move from one phase to another. With P phases this gives P − 1 equations per component, C(P − 1) in all.

unknowns   = 2 + P(C − 1)
equations  = C(P − 1)
F = unknowns − equations
  = 2 + PC − P − CP + C
  = C − P + 2
blocks.where: Each equation removes one free choice, so the degrees of freedom are the unknowns left over.

blocks.text: For a pure substance C = 1, so F = 3 − P. Because F cannot be negative, P can be at most 3: a pure substance never has four phases in equilibrium. Water has several crystal forms of ice and therefore several triple points, but no state where four phases meet.

sections.h3: Using the rule, and how it fits the state postulate

blocks.text: Superheated steam in a pipe has F = 2, so you may pick 10 bar and 250 °C independently and look up the state. Wet steam in a boiler drum has F = 1: pick 10 bar and the temperature must be 179.9 °C. At the triple point F = 0: nothing can be chosen, which is why it serves as a fixed calibration point.

With two components the count grows. A mixture of nitrogen and oxygen gas has C = 2 and P = 1, so F = 3: pressure, temperature and one mole fraction. Moist air standing over liquid water has C = 2 and P = 2, so F = 2. Fix the total pressure and the temperature, and the vapour pressure in the air is fixed at p<sub>sat</sub>(T). That is why a psychrometric chart drawn for one total pressure has just one saturation line (see 5.10).

The phase rule and the state postulate answer different questions. The phase rule counts the free intensive properties of the phases. The state postulate counts the properties needed to fix the whole state, including how much of each phase there is. For wet steam F = 1, yet two properties are still needed: p fixes T, and x then fixes v, h and s through v = v<sub>f</sub> + x(v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>).

examples.question: Use the phase rule to find the degrees of freedom, and say what you may choose, for: (a) superheated steam in a pipe; (b) wet steam in a boiler drum at 10 bar; (c) ice, water and vapour in a sealed triple-point cell; (d) moist air standing over liquid water in a closed bottle at 30 °C and 101.325 kPa, with p<sub>sat</sub>(30 °C) = 4.247 kPa. Find the humidity ratio of the air in (d). (e) Could ice, a second form of ice, liquid water and vapour coexist?
steps: (a) One component (water), one phase (vapour): F = 1 − 1 + 2 = 2. Pressure and temperature may both be chosen, for example 10 bar and 250 °C.

(b) C = 1, P = 2 (liquid and vapour): F = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1. Choosing p = 10 bar fixes T = T<sub>sat</sub> = 179.9 °C. The dryness fraction is still free, because it is an amount, not an intensive property.
(c) C = 1, P = 3: F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0. Nothing can be chosen; the cell sits at 0.01 °C and 0.6117 kPa.

(d) C = 2 (dry air and water), P = 2 (the gas phase and liquid water): F = 2 − 2 + 2 = 2. Choosing T = 30 °C and p = 101.325 kPa uses both freedoms, so the composition of the air is fixed: the air is saturated and p<sub>v</sub> = p<sub>sat</sub>(30 °C) = 4.247 kPa.
Humidity ratio of that saturated air: w = 0.622 p<sub>v</sub>/(p − p<sub>v</sub>) = 0.622 × 4.247/(101.325 − 4.247) = 2.6416/97.078 = 0.0272 kg of vapour per kg of dry air.
(e) C = 1, P = 4: F = 1 − 4 + 2 = −1. A negative F is impossible, so four phases of a pure substance cannot coexist in equilibrium.
examples.answer: (a) F = 2: choose p and T. (b) F = 1: choose p, T follows (179.9 °C at 10 bar). (c) F = 0: nothing to choose. (d) F = 2: T and p fix the air as saturated, w = 0.0272 kg/kg dry air. (e) No: F would be −1.

traps: Counting the amount of a phase, or the dryness fraction, as a degree of freedom. F counts intensive properties of the phases only.
Swapping the signs: F = C + P − 2 is wrong. Test any formula on the triple point of water, where it must give F = 0.
Counting a gas mixture as several phases. Gases always mix, so nitrogen plus oxygen is one phase, not two.
Saying p alone fixes the state of wet steam. p fixes T only; x or v is still needed to fix v, h and s.

quiz.q: State the Gibbs phase rule for a non-reacting system and name each symbol.
quiz.a: F = C − P + 2, where F is the number of degrees of freedom, C the number of components and P the number of phases in equilibrium.

quiz.q: How many degrees of freedom does water have at its triple point?
quiz.a: F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0. Temperature and pressure are both fixed, at 0.01 °C and 0.6117 kPa.

quiz.q: Why can a pure substance never show four phases in equilibrium?
quiz.a: With C = 1, F = 3 − P. Four phases would give F = −1, which means more equilibrium conditions than unknowns, so no such state can exist.

quiz.q: Wet steam has F = 1, yet steam tables need two properties to fix its state. Explain.
quiz.a: F counts intensive properties of the phases: fixing p fixes T. The proportion of vapour, x, is not counted by F but is still needed to fix the mixture’s v, h and s.

quiz.q: A sealed bottle holds liquid water, water vapour and nitrogen gas. Find F and say which properties you may choose.
quiz.a: C = 2 (water, nitrogen), P = 2 (liquid, gas): F = 2 − 2 + 2 = 2. You may choose, for example, the temperature and the total pressure; the vapour pressure is then p<sub>sat</sub>(T).

quiz.q: Derive F for C = 2 and P = 2 by counting unknowns and equations, and check it with the formula.
quiz.a: Unknowns: T and p, plus one free mole fraction in each of the two phases: 2 + 2 × 1 = 4. Equations: each of the two components has equal chemical potential in both phases: 2 × 1 = 2. F = 4 − 2 = 2, and C − P + 2 = 2 − 2 + 2 = 2.

beyond: Not for the exam. The phase rule is the backbone of phase diagrams in metallurgy (the iron–carbon diagram), ceramics and chemical engineering (azeotropes in distillation). The CALPHAD method builds such diagrams by computer from models of the Gibbs function and uses the rule to check them. Search for CALPHAD, the iron–carbon phase diagram and Duhem’s theorem to go further.
